title: Department Top Earners
scenario: A campus hiring recruiter at Razorpay wants to find employees who have the highest salary in each department.
requirements: Join the Employee table with the Department table on departmentId.
Filter for employees whose salary equals the maximum salary in their department.
Output Department Name, Employee Name, and Salary.
starterQuery:
-- Find highest earner per department
SELECT 
  d.name AS Department,
  e.name AS Employee,
  e.salary AS Salary
FROM Employee e
JOIN Department d ON e.departmentId = d.id
WHERE
solutionQuery: SELECT d.name AS Department, e.name AS Employee, e.salary AS Salary FROM Employee e JOIN Department d ON e.departmentId = d.id WHERE (e.departmentId, e.salary) IN (SELECT departmentId, MAX(salary) FROM Employee GROUP BY departmentId);

hints.text: Group the employee table by departmentId to find the maximum salary.
Filter using WHERE (departmentId, salary) IN (...).

title: Second Highest Salary
scenario: Determine the second highest distinct salary from the Employee table. If no second highest salary exists, return NULL.
requirements: Select the maximum distinct salary that is strictly less than the overall maximum salary.
Alias the result as SecondHighestSalary.
starterQuery:
-- Return the second highest distinct salary
SELECT 
  MAX(salary) AS SecondHighestSalary
FROM Employee
WHERE
solutionQuery: SELECT MAX(salary) AS SecondHighestSalary FROM Employee WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Employee);

hints.text: Find the maximum salary first using an inner subquery.
Select MAX(salary) with WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary)).

title: Employees Earning More Than Their Managers
scenario: Find employees who earn more than their direct manager in an organization hierarchy.
requirements: Perform a self-join on the Employee table where employee.managerId = manager.id.
Compare employee.salary > manager.salary.
Output the employee name aliased as Employee.
starterQuery:
-- Find employees earning more than their manager
SELECT 
  e.name AS Employee
FROM Employee e
JOIN Employee m ON e.managerId = m.id
WHERE
solutionQuery: SELECT e.name AS Employee FROM Employee e JOIN Employee m ON e.managerId = m.id WHERE e.salary > m.salary;

hints.text: Use a self-join where alias 'e' is employee and alias 'm' is manager.

title: Duplicate Emails
scenario: Find all duplicate emails registered in a customer accounts table.
requirements: Group records by email.
Filter groups having a count greater than 1 using HAVING.
Output the email column.
starterQuery:
-- Report all duplicate emails
SELECT email
FROM Person
GROUP BY email
HAVING
solutionQuery: SELECT email FROM Person GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(email) > 1;

hints.text: Combine GROUP BY email with HAVING COUNT(email) > 1.

title: Customers Who Never Order
scenario: Find all customers who have never placed an order in the e-commerce store.
requirements: Left join Customers with Orders on customerId.
Filter for records where Orders.id IS NULL.
Alias customer name as Customers.
starterQuery:
-- Customers with zero orders
SELECT 
  c.name AS Customers
FROM Customers c
LEFT JOIN Orders o ON c.id = o.customerId
WHERE
solutionQuery: SELECT c.name AS Customers FROM Customers c LEFT JOIN Orders o ON c.id = o.customerId WHERE o.id IS NULL;

hints.text: Use a LEFT JOIN and filter where the right table foreign key IS NULL.

title: Delete Duplicate Emails
scenario: Delete all duplicate emails keeping only one unique email with the smallest id.
requirements: Perform a self-join where p1.email = p2.email and p1.id > p2.id.
Filter or delete the higher id records.
starterQuery:
-- Select rows that should be retained (smallest id per email)
SELECT 
  MIN(id) AS id, email
FROM Person
GROUP BY email
ORDER BY id ASC;
solutionQuery: SELECT MIN(id) AS id, email FROM Person GROUP BY email ORDER BY id ASC;

hints.text: Group by email and select the MIN(id).

title: Rising Temperature
scenario: Find all dates' IDs with higher temperatures compared to its previous dates (yesterday).
requirements: Join Weather with itself where w1.recordDate = w2.recordDate + 1 day.
Check condition w1.temperature > w2.temperature.
Output the w1.id.
starterQuery:
-- Weather id with temperature higher than previous day
SELECT 
  w1.id
FROM Weather w1
JOIN Weather w2 ON date(w1.recordDate, '-1 day') = w2.recordDate
WHERE
solutionQuery: SELECT w1.id FROM Weather w1 JOIN Weather w2 ON date(w1.recordDate, '-1 day') = w2.recordDate WHERE w1.temperature > w2.temperature;

hints.text: Compare each record with the record exactly one day prior.

title: Top 3 Department Salaries
scenario: A high-frequency interview question from Amazon and Goldman Sachs: Find the employees who earn the top three unique salaries in each department.
requirements: Calculate dense rank of salary partitioned by departmentId ordered by salary DESC.
Filter for ranking <= 3.
Join with Department to output Department, Employee, Salary.
starterQuery:
-- Find top 3 unique salaries per department
WITH Ranked AS (
  SELECT 
    d.name AS Department,
    e.name AS Employee,
    e.salary AS Salary,
    DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY e.departmentId ORDER BY e.salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM Employee e
  JOIN Department d ON e.departmentId = d.id
)
SELECT Department, Employee, Salary
FROM Ranked
WHERE
solutionQuery: WITH Ranked AS (SELECT d.name AS Department, e.name AS Employee, e.salary AS Salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY e.departmentId ORDER BY e.salary DESC) AS rnk FROM Employee e JOIN Department d ON e.departmentId = d.id) SELECT Department, Employee, Salary FROM Ranked WHERE rnk <= 3 ORDER BY Department, Salary DESC;

hints.text: Use DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY departmentId ORDER BY salary DESC).
Filter rnk <= 3 in an outer query.

title: Rank Scores
scenario: Rank scores in descending order. If there is a tie, both scores should have the same ranking, and the next ranking should be consecutive (no gaps).
requirements: Use DENSE_RANK() ordered by score descending.
Output score and rank columns.
starterQuery:
-- Rank scores consecutively
SELECT 
  score,
  DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS rank
FROM Scores
ORDER BY score DESC;
solutionQuery: SELECT score, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS rank FROM Scores ORDER BY score DESC;

hints.text: DENSE_RANK() guarantees no gaps between consecutive numbers on ties.

title: Consecutive Numbers
scenario: Find all numbers that appear at least three times consecutively in a telemetry logs table.
requirements: Use LAG and LEAD functions or multi-table join on sequential IDs.
Filter where current = prev and current = next.
Return distinct numbers aliased as ConsecutiveNums.
starterQuery:
-- Find numbers appearing 3 times consecutively
SELECT DISTINCT num AS ConsecutiveNums
FROM (
  SELECT num, 
         LAG(num) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS prev_num,
         LEAD(num) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS next_num
  FROM Logs
)
WHERE
solutionQuery: SELECT DISTINCT num AS ConsecutiveNums FROM (SELECT num, LAG(num) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS prev_num, LEAD(num) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS next_num FROM Logs) WHERE num = prev_num AND num = next_num;

hints.text: LAG(num, 1) and LEAD(num, 1) let you inspect neighboring rows without expensive joins.

title: Average Selling Price
scenario: Calculate the average selling price for each product. Total price divided by total units sold.
requirements: Join Prices with UnitsSold where purchase_date is between start_date and end_date.
Calculate ROUND(SUM(price * units) / SUM(units), 2).
Group by product_id.
starterQuery:
-- Average selling price per product
SELECT 
  p.product_id,
  ROUND(SUM(p.price * u.units) * 1.0 / SUM(u.units), 2) AS average_price
FROM Prices p
JOIN UnitsSold u ON p.product_id = u.product_id 
  AND u.purchase_date BETWEEN p.start_date AND p.end_date
GROUP BY p.product_id;
solutionQuery: SELECT p.product_id, ROUND(SUM(p.price * u.units) * 1.0 / SUM(u.units), 2) AS average_price FROM Prices p JOIN UnitsSold u ON p.product_id = u.product_id AND u.purchase_date BETWEEN p.start_date AND p.end_date GROUP BY p.product_id;

hints.text: Join on product_id and check purchase_date BETWEEN start_date AND end_date.

title: Immediate Food Delivery
scenario: If the customer's preferred delivery date is the same as the order date, the order is called immediate. Find the percentage of immediate orders in customer's first orders.
requirements: Find each customer's first order date using MIN(order_date).
Calculate percentage where first order date equals customer_pref_delivery_date.
starterQuery:
-- Percentage of immediate first orders
WITH FirstOrders AS (
  SELECT customer_id, MIN(order_date) AS min_date
  FROM Delivery
  GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT 
  ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN d.order_date = d.customer_pref_delivery_date THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS immediate_percentage
FROM Delivery d
JOIN FirstOrders fo ON d.customer_id = fo.customer_id AND d.order_date = fo.min_date;
solutionQuery: WITH FirstOrders AS (SELECT customer_id, MIN(order_date) AS min_date FROM Delivery GROUP BY customer_id) SELECT ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN d.order_date = d.customer_pref_delivery_date THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS immediate_percentage FROM Delivery d JOIN FirstOrders fo ON d.customer_id = fo.customer_id AND d.order_date = fo.min_date;

hints.text: Isolate the first order per customer using a CTE with MIN(order_date).

title: Fix Names in a Table
scenario: Fix customer names so that only the first character is uppercase and the rest of the characters are lowercase.
requirements: Use UPPER(SUBSTR(name, 1, 1)) || LOWER(SUBSTR(name, 2)).
Order results by user_id ascending.
starterQuery:
-- Format names with first letter capitalized
SELECT 
  user_id,
  UPPER(SUBSTR(name, 1, 1)) || LOWER(SUBSTR(name, 2)) AS name
FROM Users
ORDER BY user_id ASC;
solutionQuery: SELECT user_id, UPPER(SUBSTR(name, 1, 1)) || LOWER(SUBSTR(name, 2)) AS name FROM Users ORDER BY user_id ASC;

hints.text: Concatenate UPPER of first character with LOWER of the substring from index 2.

title: Project Employees Analysis
scenario: Report the average experience years of all the employees for each project rounded to 2 digits.
requirements: Join Project with Employee on employee_id.
Calculate ROUND(AVG(experience_years), 2).
Group by project_id.
starterQuery:
-- Average experience years per project
SELECT 
  p.project_id,
  ROUND(AVG(e.experience_years), 2) AS average_years
FROM Project p
JOIN Employee e ON p.employee_id = e.employee_id
GROUP BY p.project_id;
solutionQuery: SELECT p.project_id, ROUND(AVG(e.experience_years), 2) AS average_years FROM Project p JOIN Employee e ON p.employee_id = e.employee_id GROUP BY p.project_id;

hints.text: Group by project_id and apply AVG(experience_years).

title: Recyclable and Low Fat Products
scenario: Find the product IDs of products that are both low fat ('Y') and recyclable ('Y').
requirements: Filter products where low_fats = 'Y' AND recyclable = 'Y'.
Output product_id.
starterQuery:
-- Products both low fat and recyclable
SELECT product_id
FROM Products
WHERE
solutionQuery: SELECT product_id FROM Products WHERE low_fats = 'Y' AND recyclable = 'Y';

hints.text: Apply a simple WHERE clause with AND condition.

title: Calculate Special Bonus
scenario: Calculate 100% bonus for employees whose employee_id is an odd number and name does NOT start with 'M'. Bonus is 0 otherwise.
requirements: Use CASE WHEN employee_id % 2 = 1 AND name NOT LIKE 'M%' THEN salary ELSE 0 END.
Order by employee_id ASC.
starterQuery:
-- Compute bonus based on employee id and name
SELECT 
  employee_id,
  CASE 
    WHEN employee_id % 2 = 1 AND name NOT LIKE 'M%' THEN salary 
    ELSE 0 
  END AS bonus
FROM Employees
ORDER BY employee_id ASC;
solutionQuery: SELECT employee_id, CASE WHEN employee_id % 2 = 1 AND name NOT LIKE 'M%' THEN salary ELSE 0 END AS bonus FROM Employees ORDER BY employee_id ASC;

hints.text: Use modulo operator (%) and NOT LIKE 'M%' inside CASE WHEN.

title: Swap Salary
scenario: Swap all 'f' and 'm' sex values in a salary table (i.e. change 'm' to 'f' and 'f' to 'm').
requirements: Use CASE WHEN sex = 'm' THEN 'f' ELSE 'm' END.
Output id, name, updated sex, and salary.
starterQuery:
-- Swap sex values
SELECT 
  id, name,
  CASE WHEN sex = 'm' THEN 'f' ELSE 'm' END AS sex,
  salary
FROM Salary
ORDER BY id ASC;
solutionQuery: SELECT id, name, CASE WHEN sex = 'm' THEN 'f' ELSE 'm' END AS sex, salary FROM Salary ORDER BY id ASC;

hints.text: A single CASE statement handles swapping between two values.

title: Game Play Analysis I
scenario: Find the first login date for each gamer player in an activity tracking table.
requirements: Group by player_id.
Extract MIN(event_date) aliased as first_login.
starterQuery:
-- First login date for each player
SELECT 
  player_id,
  MIN(event_date) AS first_login
FROM Activity
GROUP BY player_id
ORDER BY player_id ASC;
solutionQuery: SELECT player_id, MIN(event_date) AS first_login FROM Activity GROUP BY player_id ORDER BY player_id ASC;

hints.text: GROUP BY player_id with MIN(event_date).

title: Find Total Time Spent by Each Employee
scenario: Calculate the total time in minutes spent by each employee on each day at the office (out_time - in_time).
requirements: Group by event_day and emp_id.
Calculate SUM(out_time - in_time) aliased as total_time.
Alias event_day as day.
starterQuery:
-- Total time in minutes per employee per day
SELECT 
  event_day AS day,
  emp_id,
  SUM(out_time - in_time) AS total_time
FROM Employees
GROUP BY event_day, emp_id
ORDER BY day ASC, emp_id ASC;
solutionQuery: SELECT event_day AS day, emp_id, SUM(out_time - in_time) AS total_time FROM Employees GROUP BY event_day, emp_id ORDER BY day ASC, emp_id ASC;

hints.text: Group by both event_day and emp_id, summing the difference between out_time and in_time.

title: Sales Analysis III
scenario: Report the products that were only sold in the first quarter of 2025 (between 2025-01-01 and 2025-03-31 inclusive).
requirements: Join Product with Sales on product_id.
Ensure MIN(sale_date) >= '2025-01-01' AND MAX(sale_date) <= '2025-03-31'.
Output product_id and product_name.
starterQuery:
-- Products sold exclusively in Q1 2025
SELECT 
  p.product_id,
  p.product_name
FROM Product p
JOIN Sales s ON p.product_id = s.product_id
GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name
HAVING MIN(s.sale_date) >= '2025-01-01' AND MAX(s.sale_date) <= '2025-03-31';
solutionQuery: SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name FROM Product p JOIN Sales s ON p.product_id = s.product_id GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name HAVING MIN(s.sale_date) >= '2025-01-01' AND MAX(s.sale_date) <= '2025-03-31';

hints.text: Group by product and use HAVING with MIN(sale_date) and MAX(sale_date).
